questions.q: Which button opens Power Query Editor from the Home ribbon?
options: Transform data
Get data
Publish
Refresh
questions.explain: Transform Data opens the editor instead of loading the data straight into the report — the same choice you've been skipping past since Lesson 4 in favor of Load.

questions.q: What does the Query Settings pane's Applied Steps list actually represent?
options: An ordered, replayable recipe of every transformation applied to the query
A log of errors encountered while loading data
A list of every column in the table, regardless of transformations
A history of who edited the query and when
questions.explain: Applied Steps records each transformation in order. It's not a one-time edit log — it's a recipe that reruns automatically every time the data refreshes.

questions.q: Does Power Query change your original source data?
options: No — it records steps and replays them on whatever data shows up next, leaving the source untouched
Yes, every transformation is written back to the source file or database
Only if you select "Save to source" explicitly
Only for Excel and CSV sources, not databases
questions.explain: Power Query never modifies the source. It builds a sequence of steps and reapplies that sequence to the current data on each refresh — the core idea behind this entire chapter.

questions.q: What language are Applied Steps actually written in, viewable through Advanced Editor?
options: Power Query M
DAX
SQL
Python
questions.explain: Every ribbon action and right-click transformation generates Power Query M code behind the scenes. DAX (Chapter 5) is a separate language, used for measures and calculations, not data shaping.

options: Leaves Power Query Editor and loads the transformed data into your report
Saves the M code to a file without loading any data
Permanently overwrites the original source file
Publishes the report to the Power BI service
questions.explain: Close & Apply exits the editor and brings the transformed result into your report's model — the equivalent of Load, but after you've shaped the data first.
